newsitem.title: USA: Vanadium prices to soften up by year end - Bear.
newsitem.headline: Vanadium prices to soften up by year end - Bear.

text.p: The delicate supply and demand balance in vanadium is set to continue throughout the year with prices remaining firm until they begin to ease in the second half, Kevin Jones of Bear Metallurgical said.

The Western world vanadium market is in slight oversupply, with demand last year at 132 million pounds of vanadium pentoxide equivalent, while supply was 133 million pounds, Jones told Ryan's Notes vanadium, molybdenum and columbium conference.
Little or no inventories are held by producers, he added.

"This narrow margin leaves prices susceptible to fluctuations as a result of minor disruptions of supply from China and Russia, or a small increase in demand could also create a shortage," Jones said.
"But I don't see any major, runaway market," he added later.
Capacity was estimated at 210 million pounds a year, with utilisation rate at 63 percent last year.
Consumption of vanadium by the steel industry was expected to continue rising by three to four percent a year.
Vanadium prices began to rise earlier this year due to increased demand and constricted supply, Jones said.
"This appears to be the third rally since 1988," Jones added.

The average pentoxide and ferro-vanadium prices in the past ten years were $3.08 and $7.24 per pound respectively, a level which makes pentoxide production and conversion into ferro-vanadium viable, and the threat of substitutions only a distant possiblity.
These average prices "appear to be a good forecast for the next five years average prices," Jones said.

But the premium paid for ferro-vanadium over pentoxide, or the price paid for conversion, is set to narrow further over coming years, Jones said. The spread has averaged $1.29 since January last year, compared to $1.32 in the period since 1992.

"Long term these low pentoxide to ferro spreads cannot continue or will become meaningless because some of the conversion cost will implicitly become a built in component of the pentoxide price," Jones said.
The spread will also narrow as more vanadium trioxide is used to make ferro vanadium.
But if aluminum prices soar as some analysts have predicted, conversion costs will increase, as the former is used in the process, Jones cautioned.
It appears that most converters are covered for the year in their pentoxide requirements and that Chinese pentoxide is beginning to become more plentiful.

"Based on this I would expect the prices to remain firm for the most of 1997 with some downward pressure in the second half of theyear, with prices settling to the $3.50 range by year's end," Jones said.

He also suggested that vanadium pentoxide prices may no longer be a good indicator of the vanadium market since the South Africans began moving downstream to use their pentoxide to make ferro-vanadium, whose price may now be a better indicator.

The South Africans were still selling pentoxide to U.S. ferro producers, while producing ferro for sale themselves in the American market. "These roles may not necessarily be complementary," Jones said.
Overall supply in the vanadium market will be in balance with projected growth in demand, as added supply comes from increased recycling of ashes, residues and spent catalysts, Jones said.
